=== CALL C0173 ===
Danuta: Hello! Hello, can you hear me? Oh good, there you are. I'm Danuta.
Craig: Hi, Danuta. Craig. Yes, I can hear you fine.
Danuta: Lovely. So we have three minutes, no? I never know what to say in three minutes, I talk too much, so you stop me. Have you had your tea yet?
Craig: Not yet, no. I'll have dinner after this. Probably chicken and rice.
Danuta: Chicken and rice, very good, very healthy. I had a late shift yesterday so today I am off, I made pierogi at the weekend, sixty of them, all in the freezer now. So tonight is easy, just boil.
Craig: Sixty. That's commitment.
Danuta: My husband says I cook for an army, but then my son comes from Manchester with his little girl and they all disappear, you know? Where are you from, Craig? Your accent, it's not from here, I think.
Craig: No. Durban originally. South Africa. I've been here about twenty-four years though. I'm in Woodley, near Reading.
Danuta: Oh, South Africa! So far. I am from Poland, near Rzeszów, but I live in Preston now nearly twenty years. So we are both, how do you say, from somewhere else.
Craig: Ja, that's about right.
Danuta: And what work you do? I guessed from your photo, I think engineer, with the books and the folders.
Craig: That's right, actually. Structural engineer. Mostly refurbishment jobs. Old buildings, checking whether they'll stand up when people knock walls out.
Danuta: Ha, I was right! I'm proud of myself. I work at the hospital, I clean the wards. Eleven years on the same two wards. Everybody knows me, the nurses, the patients. I like it, but my knees, after an early shift, oh.
Craig: I can imagine. That's a lot of time on your feet.
Danuta: All day walking, mopping. But I like to talk to the old ones, the lonely ones, you know? Some of them nobody visits. Sorry, I talk too much.
Craig: No, that's fine. Someone's got to.
Danuta: And your family, they are still in South Africa?
Craig: My parents are, yes. In Durban. My sister's in Australia. I've got a daughter here, she's fifteen. That's her in the photo behind me.
Danuta: She's beautiful. Fifteen, oh, difficult age, no? My daughter at fifteen, I don't want to remember. Now she's in Poland again, I miss her very much.
Craig: Ja. It's hard, being far from people. I go back to see my folks every eighteen months or so. They're getting on a bit.
Danuta: My mother is eighty-four. I go every summer. Every time I leave I think, maybe last time, you know? It's not easy.
Craig: No. It's not.
Danuta: But then, phone calls every evening! Video, now, with my granddaughter, she says Polish words to me. So that helps.
Craig: That's good. My parents aren't great with video calls. Lots of foreheads.
Danuta: Ha! Yes, my mother too, only her ear I see!
Craig: Do you cook South African food? Sorry, I mean, do you cook much from home? Polish food?
Danuta: All the time! Gołąbki, żurek at Easter, poppy-seed cake at Christmas. And you, you have special food from Durban?
Craig: I make biltong. Dried meat. I built a drying box in the garage. The latest batch is nearly ready, actually.
Danuta: You built a box for meat! This is very engineer. My Tadeusz would love that, he—

=== CALL C0174 ===
Callum: Alright? Can you hear me yeah?
Lauren: Yeah, I can hear you! Hiya, I'm Lauren. Sorry, me cat's just walked across the table, ignore her. Well, him. Biscuit.
Callum: Biscuit, that's a proper good name. I'm Callum. How's it going?
Lauren: Yeah, good, ta. Bit knackered. How was that puzzle thing for you? I was rubbish, I just kept clicking stuff.
Callum: Same, mate, honestly. I think I just guessed half of it. Where are you, then?
Lauren: Derby. Chaddesden. Do you know Derby?
Callum: Only 'cos of football really. I'm Plymouth, so like, Argyle.
Lauren: Oh, me dad'd love you. Me and him go to the Rams sometimes, and I'm the one who shouts at the telly. He just sits there going "calm down, Lauren".
Callum: Ha, nah, I'm the same at Home Park. If I can get a cheap ticket. Or blag someone's spare.
Lauren: So what d'you do? You at uni or something? You look young, sorry, that sounds awful.
Callum: Nah, you're alright. Yeah, second year, business and management. And I work at a pub on the Barbican, glass collecting, pot washing, that sort of thing. Weekends mostly.
Lauren: Oh, nice. Do you get good tips?
Callum: Sometimes, yeah. Had a stag do in last weekend, they were proper generous, like. Bunged me a twenty for basically just being there.
Lauren: Twenty quid! That's amazing. I used to be a fitness instructor, at the leisure centre, but erm, they changed who runs it and they cut loads of classes, so my job sort of went. So I'm, you know, looking. I do the odd cover class. Signing on, the glamorous life.
Callum: Ah, that's rubbish, sorry. What kind of classes was it?
Lauren: Zumba, step, circuits. I love it, I love being at the front, getting all the nervous ones going, do you know what I mean? Like the older ladies who come in all scared and then six weeks later they're giving it everything.
Callum: That's quite cool, actually. I've got a gym membership. I use it, like, in bursts.
Lauren: Everyone does! Three weeks keen and then gone. I can always tell.
Callum: Yeah, nah, that's me exactly, caught out. What else d'you get up to, then?
Lauren: Erm, charity shops, I'm obsessed. I got a nineties windbreaker last week for three quid, proper retro, all purple and teal.
Callum: Three quid? Mate, you need to be flipping that. I do Vinted, trainers mostly. Got some Jordans the other week, made forty quid on them.
Lauren: Shut up, forty quid?
Callum: Yeah, I've got a bit of a system going. Buy cheap, clean them up, sell. A nineties windbreaker, people'd go mad for that.
Lauren: I'm not selling it though, I look amazing in it! Sorry, I'm going off on one. But that's actually a good shout, like, the ones I don't wear.
Callum: You should, honestly. Easy money. You could do, like, a whole retro page.
Lauren: Maybe. Me boyfriend Ryan'd be chuffed, he says the spare room's just bags of clothes now. So what do you wanna do after uni?
Callum: Erm, kind of sales, maybe. Or start something. Haven't really worked it out yet, I'll be—

=== CALL C0175 ===
Darren: Hello? Is it on?
Bethany: Hiya. Yeah, I think so. I can see you.
Darren: Right. Good. Darren. Not done one of these before.
Bethany: Me neither. I'm Bethany. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous.
Darren: You're alright. It's only three minutes, love. Where are you, then?
Bethany: Pontefract.
Darren: Pontefract? Give over. I'm Castleford. Born in Pontefract hospital, actually.
Bethany: Oh, no way. That's... that's mad, that. I worked in Castleford, at a flower shop. On the main road down near the precinct.
Darren: Not the one that shut? Little independent place?
Bethany: Yeah. That one. About eighteen month ago now.
Darren: I knew it. I used to drive past it in the van every day. Shame, that. It were a nice shop.
Bethany: It was. It was sort of my place, you know. I've not really found anything since, so I'm just... erm, looking. Sort of.
Darren: It's hard round here. Everything's shutting. What did you do there, then? Bouquets and that?
Bethany: Yeah, bouquets, weddings, buttonholes. And I did a lot of the sympathy flowers, for funerals. People are upset when they come in, and I didn't mind. I'd just let them talk.
Darren: Takes a certain kind of person, that. When me mam died, the lass who did the flowers were dead kind. Made a big difference, actually.
Bethany: I'm sorry about your mam.
Darren: Ah, it's three year ago now. Anyway. What about you, are you married? Sorry, saw the photo.
Bethany: Yeah, I am. My husband's called Craig. He'd like you, I think. He's Cas Tigers mad. I saw your throw in your photo.
Darren: Ha, did you? Good man. Is he going Sunday?
Bethany: He's on nights this week, so I don't know. I sit with him when he watches it on telly. I don't really understand it.
Darren: Neither do the refs, half the time. Last week were a disgrace. Sorry, I'm just being a grump.
Bethany: No, that's alright. He says the same thing every week.
Darren: I'm a joiner, by the way. Housing association. Doors, windows, kitchens, boarding up. All over Wakefield district.
Bethany: Oh, that's handy. Our back door sticks all the time. Mabel, that's our dog, she's a whippet, she's scared of it. She's scared of everything, really. The bin lorry especially.
Darren: Is that her on the settee in the back?
Bethany: Yeah, that's her. She just sleeps all day.
Darren: Lucky her. Your door'll be the frame dropping. Probably the hinges, nine times out of ten. Easy fix.
Bethany: Really? Craig keeps saying he'll look at it.
Darren: They all say that. I've been saying I'll do me own guttering since October.
Bethany: Ha. I do little pressed flowers, framed ones, for people. I could swap you one for...

=== CALL C0176 ===
Danuta: Hello! Hello, Darren, yes? I'm Danuta. Can you hear me okay?
Darren: Yeah, I can hear you. Alright.
Danuta: Good, good. This is my second one, I'm getting better I think. First one I talk too much. Have you had your tea?
Darren: Not yet. Probably just a pie and oven chips. Can't be bothered cooking just for me, you know.
Darren: Sorry, that sounds a bit sad, dunt it.
Danuta: No! Is normal. When my husband is on late, I also eat just bread and cheese standing in the kitchen. Where are you, Darren?
Darren: Castleford. West Yorkshire. You?
Danuta: Preston. But I'm from Poland, near Rzeszów. Twenty years nearly here. I clean on the wards at the hospital.
Darren: Oh right. Hard graft, that.
Danuta: Is hard on the knees. After an early shift I come home and I sit and I don't move, my husband has to bring me a brew.
Darren: Tell me about it. I'm a joiner, I'm kneeling on floors all day, fitting boards and that. Me knees are knackered by about two o'clock.
Danuta: So we are the same! Old knees club.
Darren: Ha. Yeah. Something like that.
Danuta: I liked your photo. The socks on the radiator, I laughed, sorry. My Tadeusz does exactly this.
Darren: Oh God, did you see them? I didn't even think. Live on me own, nobody to tell me off.
Danuta: And the photo on the wall, the lady at the seaside, this is your mum?
Darren: Yeah. Me mam, with me sister's kids. Bridlington, I think. She died three year ago.
Danuta: Oh, I'm sorry, love.
Darren: Ta. It's alright. I've still got all her stuff in boxes in the back bedroom. Can't sort of face going through it yet. Daft, really.
Danuta: Not daft. Not daft at all. When my father died, my mother kept his coat on the door for, oh, five years. Nobody was allowed to touch.
Darren: Yeah. That's it, innit. You just leave it.
Danuta: She's eighty-four now, my mother, in Poland. I worry all the time. I go every summer, I come back and I cry on the plane, you know?
Darren: I'm not surprised. That's a long way to be. Must be hard.
Danuta: I go to the Polish Mass on Sunday, I light a candle for her, it helps me a bit. Maybe silly.
Darren: No, it's not. I go at Christmas, and on the day she died, I sort of... yeah. I'm not much of a churchgoer, but I believe in something, do you know what I mean.
Danuta: Yes. I know exactly. It's good to have something.
Darren: Anyway. Sorry, bit heavy for three minutes, that.
Danuta: No, no, I like it. Better than talking about weather! So what you do when you are not working? You like the rugby, I think? I saw a blanket.
Darren: Cas Tigers, yeah. Rugby league. Lost again Sunday. I were in a mood all Monday.
Danuta: My husband the same with football! If Poland loses, I don't talk to him for one day, is safer.
Darren: Probably wise, that. I go fishing as well, in summer. Fairburn Ings. Just sit there. Nobody bothers you.
Danuta: That sounds peaceful. You should bring your tea, a nice barm, make a day.
Darren: Barm? Is that a Lancashire thing?
Danuta: Yes! Bacon barm, from the canteen. I learned it at the hospital, now I can't stop saying—

=== CALL C0177 ===
Lauren: Hiya! Oh, it's you, with the dog! I loved your photo. Is she there now?
Bethany: Hiya. Erm, yeah, she's just... she's under the throw, you can probably see her nose.
Lauren: Oh my God, I can, bless her! What's her name?
Bethany: Mabel. She's a whippet. She's a bit anxious, she's scared of the bin lorry.
Lauren: Aw. Mine's Biscuit, the fat grey one, he's somewhere knocking things off the windowsill. I'm Lauren, by the way, sorry, I just went straight in.
Bethany: That's alright. I'm Bethany. I saw your cat as well, in the photo.
Lauren: Did you? He gets everywhere. So where are you, duck?
Bethany: Pontefract. In Yorkshire.
Lauren: Oh, not that far then, I'm Derby. My last call was with a lad from Plymouth, I didn't even know where to start with that. He was nice, though, bit cheeky.
Bethany: Mine was a man from Castleford. That's like next door to me. He knew the flower shop I used to work at.
Lauren: No way! Small world. So you're a florist?
Bethany: I was. The shop closed, eighteen month ago. So I'm not really doing anything at the minute. Just... looking. Sorry.
Lauren: Don't say sorry! Honestly, I'm the same, I was a fitness instructor at the leisure centre and they handed it to some new company and cut the timetable and that was me, gone. Five months now. I'm signing on and everything.
Bethany: Oh no. That's horrible.
Lauren: It is, it's proper rubbish. I tell people and I sort of laugh it off, but, you know. You feel a bit daft, don't you? Like everyone else has got somewhere to be.
Bethany: Yeah. That's exactly it. My husband does long shifts and I'm just at home with the dog, and I feel a bit, erm, useless sometimes.
Lauren: You're not useless! You do flowers, that's a skill. I couldn't arrange a bunch of daffs to save my life.
Bethany: I do still do bits. Weddings for friends. And I press flowers, I make little framed ones. Them on the shelf behind me.
Lauren: Oh, are they yours? They look lovely, I thought you'd bought them. You should be selling them! Like at craft fairs, or online.
Bethany: I've thought about it. Doing wedding flowers from home and that. But I'm rubbish with the paperwork side. And websites. I don't know, it's just... a lot.
Lauren: Oh, same, same! I want to do my own dance classes, for women and older ladies, in church halls and that, and I keep saying I'll do a start-up course at the job centre. Have I booked it? Have I heck.
Bethany: Ha. I've got a wedding planning course I never finished.
Lauren: We're as bad as each other! We should do it together, like, kick each other up the bum.
Bethany: Maybe. That'd be nice, actually.
Lauren: Sorry, I'm going off on one. What are you having for your tea?
Bethany: Erm, just sausage and mash, I think. Craig's on nights so it's just me.
Lauren: Same here, Ryan's on shifts, so it'll be a cheese cob for me. Again. Living the dream, duck.
Bethany: Ha. I made a banana bread yesterday, it sank in the middle, so I might just have that.
Lauren: Sunk ones taste better, everyone knows that, it's all the gooey—

=== CALL C0178 ===
Darren: Hello? Right, I can see you. Darren.
Craig: Hi, Darren. Craig.
Darren: Alright. Third one of these now. Getting the hang of it, sort of.
Craig: Ja, same. They go quickly.
Darren: They do. Where are you, then? You don't sound local to anywhere I know.
Craig: Woodley. Near Reading. Originally Durban, South Africa, but I've been here twenty-four years.
Darren: Oh, right. I'm Castleford, West Yorkshire. I've hardly been further south than Leicester. What do you do?
Craig: Structural engineer. Mostly refurbishment. Old buildings, people wanting walls taken out, that sort of thing.
Darren: Ha. So you're the bloke who says whether we can knock through. I'm a joiner. Housing association, all the social housing round Wakefield. Doors, windows, kitchens, floorboards, boarding up after break-ins.
Craig: So you're the one who actually does it.
Darren: Somebody has to. No offence, but half the drawings we get, you look at them and think, has this fella ever stood in a house?
Craig: None taken. I review contractor drawings. I think the same about some of those.
Darren: Ha! Fair enough. It's the uPVC frames that get me, though. Whoever designed them wants a word.
Craig: Er, what's the problem with them?
Darren: They're cheap, that's the problem. Hinges go, the door drops, it won't lock, tenant rings up, and I'm the one stood there in the rain with a screwdriver because the scheduling system's sent me to the wrong end of Normanton first. Sorry, I'm just being a grump.
Craig: No, that's fair. We had a new software rollout in March. Changed everything for no reason. Took me a month to get back to where I was.
Darren: Always the way, that. Do they ask the people who actually use it? Do they heck.
Craig: No. They don't.
Darren: You into your rugby? I saw a Springboks mug on your shelf.
Craig: Ja. I watch every test. Not sure the squad's that good this year, mind.
Darren: Union, though. Well, nobody's perfect. I'm league. Cas Tigers. Lost again Sunday.
Craig: Sorry to hear that.
Darren: Ref were a disgrace. Anyway. What else do you do, when you're not doing your sums?
Craig: Cycle. Weekend mornings, on my own. Same few loops out towards Wargrave and Henley. And I make biltong in the garage. Dried meat.
Darren: Oh, I know biltong. Lad at work brought some in once. Proper good, that. You make it yourself?
Craig: I built a drying box. Light bulb and a computer fan, basically. This batch is nearly done.
Darren: That's grand, that. I've got a shed, I make bits out of offcuts. Bird boxes and that. Built me sister a bench for her garden last year.
Craig: That's good. Nice to make something you can actually use.
Darren: That's it, yeah. Have you got family down there? Kids?
Craig: A daughter. Fifteen. She's with me every other weekend and one night a week. The rest of the time it's quiet.
Darren: Yeah. I know quiet. I live on me own an' all. You end up talking to next door's cat, do you know what I mean.
Craig: Ja. Or the TV.
Darren: Or that. Mind you, I've been meaning to sort me guttering since October, so I've got plenty to be getting on with if I could be bothered.
Craig: Mine needs doing too. It's been on the list since—

=== CALL C0179 ===
Callum: Alright? You're the one with the dog, yeah?
Bethany: Erm, yeah. Hiya. I'm Bethany.
Callum: Callum. She there now? The dog?
Bethany: She's asleep. She's always asleep. She's called Mabel.
Callum: Mabel. Love that. Proper old lady name.
Bethany: Ha. Yeah. She sort of acts like one as well.
Callum: Where's that to, then? Where are you?
Bethany: Sorry? Oh, Pontefract. Yorkshire.
Callum: Nice. I'm Plymouth. Bit of a trek. How you finding these calls, then?
Bethany: Erm, okay. I was dead nervous at first. It's getting a bit easier.
Callum: You're doing fine. I just chat rubbish, me. What do you do?
Bethany: I was a florist. The shop shut, so... not really anything at the minute. I'm looking.
Callum: Ah, that's a shame. Flowers, though, that's like a proper skill, yeah? Weddings and that?
Bethany: Yeah, weddings, funerals. I still do bits for friends. And I press flowers and frame them. Them on the shelf behind me.
Callum: Wait, you made them? I thought they were from a shop or something.
Bethany: No, they're mine. Thank you.
Callum: Mate, you could sell them. Honestly. I flip trainers on Vinted, made forty quid on some Jordans last week. People pay stupid money for handmade stuff. Etsy, Instagram, whatever.
Bethany: That's what the girl from Derby said, actually. Lauren. I spoke to her before.
Callum: Oh, Lauren! I had her first. She was a laugh. I told her to flog her windbreaker.
Bethany: Ha, she said she weren't selling it.
Callum: Yeah, she weren't having it. But seriously, you should. Take a nice picture, stick it up, see what happens.
Bethany: I don't know. It's the money side and the posting and, erm, websites. I get a bit overwhelmed. I'm not very organised, sorry.
Callum: Nah, you're alright. I'm not organised either, I just wing it. I've had like four extensions at uni this year.
Bethany: Four? Do they let you?
Callum: If you ask nicely, yeah. I'm doing business and management, second year. Don't tell my mum about the extensions, she thinks I'm a genius.
Bethany: Ha. I won't. Is it good, the course?
Callum: It's alright. Bit boring. I'm kind of not sure, to be honest. I work at a pub as well, weekends, so I'm proper knackered by Monday.
Bethany: My husband's on nights this week. He's the same, he just sleeps all day like Mabel.
Callum: Ha, him and the dog. What's for your tea, then? Everyone keeps asking that on these.
Bethany: Erm, sausage and mash. Or banana bread. I made one and it sank.
Callum: Banana bread for tea, that's a power move, that.
Bethany: Ha. What about you?
Callum: Whatever Mum makes. If it's salad, I'm getting Greggs. Or an air fryer job, I can—

=== CALL C0180 ===
Danuta: Hello! Oh, it's you, the girl with the beautiful smile! I'm Danuta.
Lauren: Aw, hiya! I'm Lauren. Oh, I've been wanting to talk to you, I saw your photo and I thought, she looks lovely, she'd make you a brew.
Danuta: Of course I make you a brew! And cake. Have you had your tea yet, love?
Lauren: Not yet, it'll be a cheese cob, honestly, me boyfriend's on shifts so I don't bother. Where are you, duck?
Danuta: Preston. But I'm from Poland, near Rzeszów. You?
Lauren: Derby. Chaddesden. What do you do?
Danuta: I clean at the hospital, on the wards. Eleven years same two wards. I love the patients, the old ladies, they tell me all their stories. But my knees, oh, after an early shift, finished.
Lauren: Oh, that's me old job sort of! Not the cleaning, I mean the older ladies. I was a fitness instructor and I loved the oldies, they were my favourites. I used to do chair classes and that, for people with dodgy knees.
Danuta: Chair classes! This exists? Maybe I need this.
Lauren: Honestly, you'd love it, it's all sat down, bit of music, arms going, nobody judges. I want to set up my own one day, in church halls round Derby. Dance for women and older ladies.
Danuta: Oh, this is a beautiful idea. In my church, in Preston, the ladies would come, I know. They love music. I sing in the choir sometimes.
Lauren: Do you? Oh, I love that. I was a dancer, I did a bit of a dance degree, but I sort of dropped out. Still annoys me, to be honest.
Danuta: You were young. When you are young you make decisions, then you go another way. Is not the end.
Lauren: Yeah. I know. I lost the job five months ago, they cut the timetable, so I'm signing on, and money's, you know... Sorry, I don't know why I'm telling you all this.
Danuta: No, no, tell me. Is hard. When we came here, my husband and me, we had nothing, I worked in a chicken factory. Now look, I'm on the ward, everybody knows my name. You will find something, I'm sure. You have a face people like.
Lauren: Oh, stop it, you'll set me off. Thank you, though. Do you watch Strictly? Tell me you watch Strictly.
Danuta: Every Saturday! My husband falls asleep, I watch alone and I shout at the judges.
Lauren: Same! I shout at the telly at the Rams and at Strictly, me dad says I'm a nightmare.
Danuta: Ha! Who you like this year?
Lauren: Oh, I'm rubbish with names, I just like the big group numbers, all the choreography. Me and me mum go to musicals at Derby Theatre when we can afford it.
Danuta: My granddaughter, she dances now, five years old, in a little pink skirt. Too beautiful.
Lauren: Aw, bless her. You need to get her in a class early, they love it at that age.
Danuta: Yes! And you come to Preston and teach the grandmas. Then my knees get better too.
Lauren: Deal. I'll need loads of tea and cake, mind.
Danuta: This is easy. I have sixty pierogi in the freezer, so you never go—

=== CALL C0181 ===
Craig: Hi. Craig.
Bethany: Hiya. I'm Bethany.
Craig: Nice to meet you. Is this your fourth?
Bethany: Erm, yeah. Fourth. I think it's the last one.
Craig: Same here. Where are you based?
Bethany: Pontefract. In Yorkshire. Sorry, I keep saying "in Yorkshire" like nobody knows where it is.
Craig: I didn't, to be honest. I'm in Woodley. Near Reading.
Bethany: Oh, right. Down south.
Craig: Ja. Originally South Africa, though. Durban.
Bethany: I thought your accent were different. That's a long way.
Craig: It is. Twenty-four years ago now.
Bethany: My husband's called Craig, actually. So that's, erm... that's easy to remember.
Craig: Good. Saves you writing it down.
Bethany: Ha. What do you do?
Craig: Structural engineer. Mostly refurbishment. Checking old buildings will stay up when people change them.
Bethany: Oh. That sounds really clever. I was a florist. The shop closed, so I'm not working at the minute.
Craig: Sorry to hear that. Was it a big shop?
Bethany: No, just a little one in Castleford. The man I spoke to earlier, Darren, he knew it. He used to drive past it.
Craig: I had Darren as well. Joiner. He wasn't keen on uPVC frames.
Bethany: Ha, no. He told me our back door's probably the hinges. Craig's been saying he'll look at it for ages.
Craig: He's probably right. Hinges drop, the door catches on the frame. Usually a few screws and some packing. Half an hour, if you've got the right screwdriver.
Bethany: Really? I might just do it myself, then. I'll look it up.
Craig: You'll be fine. Take a photo before you start, so you know how it went back.
Bethany: That's a good idea. Thank you.
Craig: Do you still do flowers at all? For yourself?
Bethany: Erm, a bit. I've got a little raised bed in the back. The peonies are coming through now, I check them every morning, which is a bit sad. And I press flowers and frame them. Them on the shelf behind me are mine.
Craig: They're nice. I thought they were bought.
Bethany: Everyone keeps saying that. Thank you. What do you do, when you're not working?
Craig: Cycle on Saturday mornings. Watch rugby. Cut the lawn more often than it needs. My daughter says I'm obsessed with it.
Bethany: How old is she?
Craig: Fifteen. She's in the school play next month. I go to all of them. I don't understand most of them, but I go.
Bethany: Aw, that's lovely. She'll remember that, you know. My dad came to everything when I was little. Even the rubbish nativity where I was a sheep.
Craig: Sounds like a strong performance.
Bethany: Ha, I had one line. Baa. I think I forgot it.
Craig: Easy to do under pressure. What are you having for dinner?
Bethany: Tea? Erm, sausage and mash. I've said that to everybody now, I'll have to actually make it.
Craig: Ja, I'm committed to chicken and rice. I've told three people.
Bethany: Ha. We'll both have to stick to it, then. Have you got far to go after this, or are you—

=== CALL C0182 ===
Lauren: Hiya! Darren, is it? I'm Lauren. Oh, you're the one with the Tigers throw!
Darren: That's me. Alright, Lauren.
Lauren: You alright, duck? How've you found these? I've loved it, honestly, I've talked the ears off everyone.

calls.C0173:
Danuta: Hello! Hello, can you hear me? Oh good, there you are. I'm Danuta.
Craig: Hi, Danuta. Craig. Yes, I can hear you fine.

Danuta: Chicken and rice, very good, very healthy. I had a late shift yesterday so today I am off, I made pierogi at the weekend, sixty of them, all in the freezer now. So tonight is easy, just boil.

Danuta: My husband says I cook for an army, but then my son comes from Manchester with his little girl and they all disappear, you know? Where are you from, Craig? Your accent, it's not from here, I think.
Craig: No. Durban originally. South Africa. I've been here about twenty-four years though. I'm in Woodley, near Reading.
Danuta: Oh, South Africa! So far. I am from Poland, near Rzeszów, but I live in Preston now nearly twenty years. So we are both, how do you say, from somewhere else.
Craig: Ja, that's about right.
Danuta: And what work you do? I guessed from your photo, I think engineer, with the books and the folders.
Craig: That's right, actually. Structural engineer. Mostly refurbishment jobs. Old buildings, checking whether they'll stand up when people knock walls out.
Danuta: Ha, I was right! I'm proud of myself. I work at the hospital, I clean the wards. Eleven years on the same two wards. Everybody knows me, the nurses, the patients. I like it, but my knees, after an early shift, oh.
Craig: I can imagine. That's a lot of time on your feet.
Danuta: All day walking, mopping. But I like to talk to the old ones, the lonely ones, you know? Some of them nobody visits. Sorry, I talk too much.
Craig: No, that's fine. Someone's got to.
Danuta: And your family, they are still in South Africa?
Craig: My parents are, yes. In Durban. My sister's in Australia. I've got a daughter here, she's fifteen. That's her in the photo behind me.
Danuta: She's beautiful. Fifteen, oh, difficult age, no? My daughter at fifteen, I don't want to remember. Now she's in Poland again, I miss her very much.
Craig: Ja. It's hard, being far from people. I go back to see my folks every eighteen months or so. They're getting on a bit.
Danuta: My mother is eighty-four. I go every summer. Every time I leave I think, maybe last time, you know? It's not easy.
Craig: No. It's not.
Danuta: But then, phone calls every evening! Video, now, with my granddaughter, she says Polish words to me. So that helps.
Craig: That's good. My parents aren't great with video calls. Lots of foreheads.
Danuta: Ha! Yes, my mother too, only her ear I see!
Craig: Do you cook South African food? Sorry, I mean, do you cook much from home? Polish food?
Danuta: All the time! Gołąbki, żurek at Easter, poppy-seed cake at Christmas. And you, you have special food from Durban?
Craig: I make biltong. Dried meat. I built a drying box in the garage. The latest batch is nearly ready, actually.
Danuta: You built a box for meat! This is very engineer. My Tadeusz would love that, he—
calls.C0174:

calls.C0175:

Bethany: Ha. I do little pressed flowers, framed ones, for people. I could swap you one for...
calls.C0176:
Danuta: Hello! Hello, Darren, yes? I'm Danuta. Can you hear me okay?

calls.C0177:

calls.C0180:

calls.C0182:

calls.C0185:

Callum: That's fine, you can mind the passports. You look like the organised one.
Darren: You've clearly not seen me van. Lost tenants' keys down the seat more than once.
Callum: Oh, so you're just like me, then, but with tools.
Darren: Don't push it, pal. Mind you, you might be right. Me sister'd say—

C0178.line_text: A daughter. Fifteen. She's with me every other weekend and one night a week. The rest of the time it's quiet.
C0178.what: As he says it, Craig briefly turns his head over his left shoulder towards the framed photo of the teenage girl on the bookshelf behind him, holds the look for a second or two, then turns back to the screen with his face unchanged.
